title: SYNTHETIC — The Tern River Mill Payroll

units.text: On the morning of November 12, 1954, the weekly payroll of the Tern River Mill was gone from the office safe.
The police report noted one detail that would shape everything after: no signs that the safe had been forced.
The cash, eighteen thousand four hundred dollars, had been locked inside the afternoon before.
At trial, the mill's office manager testified that at least three employees knew the combination.
Police focused on one of them. They alleged that the bookkeeper, Oren Tallis, had opened the safe himself.
In December 1954, he was charged with larceny.
The night watchman testified that he saw a light in the office window at about two in the morning. The local paper, the day after the theft, had reported that light shortly after midnight.
The case would turn on what the prosecution could prove, not on what it could suggest.
In March 1955, the jury acquitted Tallis. The judge's written ruling put it plainly: "Suspicion, however strong, is not proof."
Some online retellings say the case ended in a jail sentence. The court record says otherwise: the only person charged was acquitted.
As of April 1955, the payroll had not been recovered.
We found no record of anyone else being charged, though the surviving sources are thin.
Which leaves the question the court could not answer: who opened the safe?
